How was William Blake a pioneer for the Romantic era?

Blake was one of the first romantic poets. As such, he was in many ways a radical of his time, rebelling against the rapid modernisation, advance -but not progress- of society. As a 'radical' poet, Blake advocated for the return of man to nature, undermining the tall factories that now littered the London skyline.Blake also rebelled against conventions of his time, placing women and children as important figures within society: pure and selfless.Similarly, Blake contradicted the accepted hierarchies of his time by comparing man with animals like lambs, emphasising the idea of man as an intrinsic part of nature, not lord of it. Overall, Blake championed personal freedoms, the beauty of the natural world and the naturally altruistic disposition of man.

Blake went against the conventions of poetry at the time. Instead of using it as a demonstration of intellectual prowess, showing off knowledge of fashionable language, history and mythology, Blake used accessible language and themes relatable to all classes, in particular the working class. As a result he created a platform through which he could share his romantic ideas and philosophies, integrated into his poetry, with a much larger audience.

In what way is Blake's omission of gender in poems such as 'Infant Joy' significant to the time period he was writing in?

The fixed gender roles and stereotypes at that time were far more stringent, hence why the omission of gender is arguably more surprising than it would be today even with increased awareness over gender issues. Blake seems to make the assertion that gender in this context, or perhaps society in general, is an unimportant feature. Deconstructing these gender roles as a modern reader would be significant for different reason. To Blake it is likely he believed that if this child were a girl or a boy their innocence is what matters and therefore what should be focused on.
